title: Hubble's 1929 distances and velocities of 24 nebulae (Table 1)

object.name: Twenty-four extra-galactic nebulae
object.frame: distances in Mpc (the paper: 10^6 pc), velocities in km/s

facility.observatory: Mount Wilson (Hubble) and Lowell (Slipher) velocities, as compiled by the paper
facility.pipeline: Hubble 1929, PNAS 15, 168, Table 1, typed from the page image

credit: Hubble, E. 1929, PNAS 15, 168 (a United States work of 1929, public domain)

license.statement: Published in the United States in 1929. The US Copyright Office (Circular 15A) says every work published in the United States before 1 January 1931 is in the public domain.

columns.name: distance
columns.description: the paper's r, in megaparsecs (its unit is 10^6 pc)

columns.name: velocity
columns.description: the paper's v, a radial velocity from the nebula's lines, km/s

reductions: All 24 rows of Table 1, typed from the page image (PMC522427; pnas01016-0007.png, sha256 cc3f720d...), in the paper's order. The nebulae's names are in object.identifiers, in row order.

Checked against the paper's own printed absolute-magnitude column: M_t recomputed from m_t and r for every row. 21 rows agree within rounding; 3 (NGC 5457, 3031 and 4826) differ by 0.066 to 0.071 mag, which is the paper's arithmetic, not a typing error. The printed mean, -15.5, is reproduced as -15.483.
The paper's m_s column (blank for nine rows) and its printed M_t are not kept. Distances, velocities and magnitudes keep the paper's digits.

source.archive: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, via PubMed Central (PMC522427)

citations.text: Hubble, E. 1929, PNAS 15, 168 (A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae)

steps: Read the 24 rows typed from Table 1 (name, r, v, m_t, printed M_t).
Recompute M_t = m_t + 5 - 5 log10(r in pc) and refuse a row more than 0.075 mag from the paper's.
Store distance, velocity and m_t as table-columns/1.

assumptions: The distances are Hubble's, which were about seven times too small (the Cepheid scale of 1929 was not yet corrected for Population II stars and dust); the slope they give is not the modern Hubble constant, and the lessons say why.
The paper's solar-motion solution cannot be reproduced: the table carries no positions. A plain straight line is what the pack supports.

validation.check: a straight line through the 24 nebulae has Hubble's slope (465 +- 50 km/s/Mpc with solar motion) within the two errors, and the mean absolute magnitude is his printed -15.5 within 0.05
